pages.x: Judea was ruled by the Seleucids, Greek kings descended from one of Alexander's generals. In 167 BC King Antiochus IV, who called himself Epiphanes, God made manifest, banned Jewish practices, from circumcision to keeping the Sabbath, and set up an altar to Zeus in the Temple in Jerusalem.

In the village of Modiin an old priest, Mattathias, was ordered to make a sacrifice to the Greek gods. He refused, and when another Jew stepped forward to do it, Mattathias killed him and the king's officer, and fled to the hills with his five sons.

When Mattathias died, his son Judah took command. He was called Maccabee, probably meaning the hammer. With bands of fighters who knew the hills, he ambushed and beat one Seleucid army after another, at Beth Horon and at Emmaus.

In 164 BC Judah's men took back Jerusalem. They cleansed the Temple and dedicated it again, with eight days of celebration. Jews have marked it ever since as Hanukkah, which means dedication. A later tradition tells of a single jar of pure oil that burned for all eight days.

The war went on. At Beth Zechariah the Seleucids came with war elephants, and Judah's brother Eleazar ran beneath the largest, thinking it carried the king, and stabbed it in the belly; it fell and crushed him. In 160 BC Judah himself was killed in battle at Elasa.

Judah's brothers fought on and won full independence. Their family, the Hasmoneans, ruled Judea as priests and kings for about a century, until Rome took over. The revolt is one of the first wars on record fought for freedom of religion, and every winter Jews light the Hanukkah candles in its memory.
pts: A revolt against a ban on Judaism
The Temple was dedicated again in 164 BC
